q: In this spinal cord cross section, back side at the top, which structure does pointer 7 mark?
options: Dorsal horn
Lateral horn
Anterior column
Ventral horn

why.correct: Pointer 7 marks the broad gray horn reaching toward the front: the ventral (anterior) horn, which holds the cell bodies of motor neurons to skeletal muscle.
options: The dorsal horn is the narrow gray horn reaching toward the back, at pointer 3.
The lateral horn is the small gray bump at the side, at pointer 4.
The anterior column is white matter at the front beside the midline, at pointer 8, not gray matter.
Correct. The broad front horn of gray matter is the ventral horn.

q: Which structure does pointer 11 mark?
options: Dorsal root ganglion
Ventral root
Lateral column of white matter
Central canal

why.correct: Pointer 11 marks the swelling on the root entering the back of the cord: the dorsal root ganglion, which holds the cell bodies of sensory neurons.
options: Correct. The swelling on the dorsal root is the dorsal root ganglion.
The ventral root leaves the front of the cord, at pointer 12, and has no swelling.
The lateral column is white matter inside the cord, at pointer 5.
The central canal is the tiny hole in the center of the cord, at pointer 6.

q: Which structure does pointer 9 mark?
options: Posterior median sulcus
Anterior median fissure
Central canal
Anterior column

why.correct: Pointer 9 marks the deep, wide groove in the midline at the front of the cord: the anterior median fissure.
options: The posterior median sulcus is the shallow groove at the back, at pointer 1.
Correct. The deep front groove is the anterior median fissure.
The central canal is the tiny hole in the center, at pointer 6.
The anterior column is the white matter beside the fissure, at pointer 8, not the groove itself.

q: Which numbered structure holds the cell bodies of sympathetic motor neurons, and at what levels of the cord is it found?
options: Pointer 3, at every level
Pointer 7, only in the enlargements
Pointer 4, only from T1 to L2
Pointer 11, only in the lumbar region

why.correct: The lateral horn, the small gray bump at the side (pointer 4), holds sympathetic motor neurons. It is present only in the thoracic and upper lumbar segments, T1 to L2.
options: Pointer 3 is the dorsal horn, which is sensory and present at every level.
Pointer 7 is the ventral horn, which holds somatic motor neurons to skeletal muscle; it is largest in the enlargements but present at every level.
Correct. The lateral horn holds sympathetic neurons, from T1 to L2.
Pointer 11 is the dorsal root ganglion, which holds sensory cell bodies at every level.

q: Which structure does pointer 2 mark?
options: Dorsal horn
Lateral column
Posterior column
Posterior median sulcus

why.correct: Pointer 2 marks the white matter between the dorsal horn and the posterior median sulcus: the posterior column, made almost entirely of ascending tracts.
options: The dorsal horn is the gray matter beside it, at pointer 3.
The lateral column is the white matter at the side, between the dorsal and ventral horns, at pointer 5.
Correct. The white matter between the dorsal horn and the midline at the back is the posterior column.
The posterior median sulcus is the shallow groove in the midline at the back, at pointer 1.

q: At about what vertebral level does the spinal cord end in an adult?
options: The first to second lumbar vertebrae
The seventh cervical vertebra
The twelfth thoracic vertebra
The second sacral vertebra

why.correct: In an adult the cord tapers to the conus medullaris at about L1–L2, because the vertebral column grew longer than the cord.
options: Correct. The conus medullaris lies at about L1–L2.
The cord runs well below the neck, through the whole thoracic region.
The cord reaches a little lower than T12, into the upper lumbar region.
S2 is where the dural sac and subarachnoid space end, not the cord.

q: What is the cauda equina?
options: The cone-shaped lower end of the spinal cord
The bundle of lumbar and sacral roots hanging in the canal below the cord
The widened part of the cord that supplies the lower limbs
The thin strand of pia that continues below the cord and anchors it to the coccyx

why.correct: The cauda equina (horse's tail) is the bundle of long lumbar and sacral roots running down the vertebral canal below the end of the cord, on their way to their exit holes.
options: The cone-shaped end of the cord is the conus medullaris; the cauda equina hangs below it.
Correct. The cauda equina is roots, not cord.
The widened part supplying the lower limbs is the lumbar enlargement.
That strand of pia anchors the cord below; the cauda equina is the bundle of roots hanging around it.

q: Mr. Adeyemi, 41, has a burst disc between his fourth and fifth lumbar vertebrae. His legs are weak, the skin between his thighs is numb, and he cannot pass urine. Which structure is being compressed?
options: The conus medullaris
The cervical enlargement
The lumbar enlargement of the cord
The cauda equina

why.correct: At L4–L5 the vertebral canal holds no spinal cord, only the cauda equina: the lumbar and sacral roots on their way down. Crushing them causes leg weakness, numbness of the saddle area and loss of bladder control, a surgical emergency.
options: The conus medullaris lies at about L1–L2, above the burst disc.
The cervical enlargement is in the neck and supplies the upper limbs.
The lumbar enlargement is part of the cord and lies behind the lower thoracic vertebrae, well above L4–L5.
Correct. At L4–L5 the canal holds only the cauda equina.

q: Why is the spinal cord wider in the lower neck than in the middle of the thoracic region?
options: The lower neck segments hold more neurons for the muscles and skin of the upper limbs
The meninges are thicker in the neck to protect the cord from movement
The central canal widens in the neck to hold more cerebrospinal fluid
The vertebral canal is wider in the neck, so the cord swells to fill it

why.correct: The cervical enlargement supplies the upper limbs, which have far more muscle and skin than a stretch of trunk. Its segments hold more motor neurons and receive more sensory axons, so they have more gray matter.
options: Correct. More neurons for the limbs means more gray matter and a wider cord.
The width is the cord's own tissue, not its coverings.
The central canal is tiny everywhere and often partly closed in adults.
The cord does not swell to fill the space; its width reflects how many neurons it holds.

q: To treat severe pain, a surgeon cuts the dorsal roots of one segment on the right side. What would you expect in the area that segment supplies?
options: Paralysis of the muscles, with normal sensation
Loss of sensation, with normal muscle strength
Loss of both sensation and strength
No change, because the ventral roots carry the sensory signals

why.correct: Dorsal roots carry sensory axons into the cord; ventral roots carry motor axons out. Cutting only the dorsal roots stops sensation from that area reaching the cord, while the motor axons in the intact ventral roots still drive the muscles.
options: Paralysis with normal sensation would follow cutting the ventral roots, which carry the motor axons.
Correct. Cutting the dorsal roots removes sensation and spares strength.
Losing both would need both roots cut, or the nerve beyond where they join.
The ventral roots carry motor axons out; sensory signals enter through the dorsal roots.

q: A virus destroys motor neurons in the ventral horns of the lumbar enlargement on both sides. Predict the change in each over the following weeks.

variables.name: Strength of the leg muscles
variables.why: The lumbar enlargement's ventral horns hold the motor neurons for the legs. With them gone, fewer commands reach the leg muscles, so they weaken.

variables.name: Sensation from the skin of the legs
variables.why: Sensation enters through the dorsal roots and dorsal horns, which the virus spared, so touch and pain from the legs still reach the brain.

variables.name: Size of the leg muscles
variables.why: Muscles that no longer receive signals from their motor neurons waste away over weeks.

variables.name: Strength of the arm muscles
variables.why: The arm muscles are supplied from the cervical enlargement, which the virus did not reach.

why.correct: Ventral horn motor neurons are the only route from the cord to the skeletal muscles they supply. Destroying those in the lumbar enlargement weakens and wastes the leg muscles, while sensation (dorsal side) and the arms (cervical enlargement) are spared.

q: Which statements about the dorsal root are true? Select all that apply.
options: It carries sensory axons into the spinal cord
Its ganglion holds the cell bodies of sensory neurons
It carries motor axons out to skeletal muscles
The neurons whose cell bodies sit in its ganglion are pseudounipolar
Its cell bodies lie in the ventral horn

why.correct: The dorsal root brings sensory axons into the back of the cord. Their cell bodies sit outside the cord in the dorsal root ganglion, and the neurons are pseudounipolar: one process runs to the body, the other into the cord.
options: Yes. The dorsal root is the sensory way in.
Yes. The dorsal root ganglion holds the sensory cell bodies.
No. Motor axons leave through the ventral root.
Yes. Dorsal root ganglion neurons are pseudounipolar.
No. Ventral horn cell bodies send their axons out through the ventral root; dorsal root cell bodies sit in the ganglion.

q: Mrs. Jensen, 70, had chickenpox as a child. Now she has a painful, blistering rash in a band around the right side of her chest. Where has the virus been lying dormant?
options: In the ventral horn of the spinal cord
In a dorsal root ganglion
In the lateral horn of the spinal cord
In the posterior column

why.correct: After chickenpox the virus lies dormant in the cell bodies of sensory neurons in a dorsal root ganglion. When it reactivates as shingles, it travels out along that ganglion's sensory axons, so the rash follows the band of skin that one dorsal root supplies, on one side only.
options: Ventral horn neurons are motor neurons; the rash follows a sensory territory.
Correct. The virus hides in a dorsal root ganglion.
Lateral horn neurons are sympathetic motor neurons, not the sensory neurons whose axons reach the skin.
The posterior column holds axons running up the cord, not the cell bodies where the virus waits.

q: A cross section of spinal cord has only a thin rim of white matter around a relatively large area of gray matter, and it has no lateral horns. Which level is it most likely from?
options: Upper cervical
Middle thoracic
Upper lumbar
Sacral

why.correct: White matter thins going down the cord: fewer ascending axons have joined yet, and most descending axons have already left for their target segments. The thinnest white matter is at the sacral end, and lateral horns are absent below L2.
options: The upper cervical cord has the most white matter, since it carries every ascending and descending axon for the whole body.
Middle thoracic segments have lateral horns, which this section lacks.
Upper lumbar segments (to L2) still have lateral horns and more white matter than the sacral cord.
Correct. A thin white rim with no lateral horns fits the sacral cord.

q: You step on a tack and your leg pulls away. Put the structures the signal passes through in order, from the sole of the foot to the leg muscle.
options: Sensory axon running in from the sole
Dorsal root ganglion
Dorsal root
Dorsal horn interneuron
Ventral horn motor neuron
Ventral root

why.correct: The sensory signal runs past its cell body in the dorsal root ganglion, enters through the dorsal root and reaches the dorsal horn. An interneuron passes it to a ventral horn motor neuron, whose axon leaves through the ventral root to the muscle.
options: The sensory neuron fires in the skin of the sole.
Its cell body sits in the dorsal root ganglion, beside the path of the signal.
The central process enters the cord through the dorsal root.
In the dorsal horn, the signal passes to an interneuron.
The interneuron excites a motor neuron in the ventral horn.
The motor axon leaves through the ventral root toward the leg muscle.

q: A tract's name begins with "spino-" and ends with the name of a brain region. What does that tell you?
options: It starts in that brain region and carries motor commands down
It stays entirely within the spinal cord, linking one segment to the segments above and below it
It starts in the spinal cord and carries information up to that region
It carries signals out of the cord through the ventral roots

why.correct: Tract names give origin first and destination second. "Spino-" first means it starts in the spinal cord; the brain region second is where it ends. So it is ascending and carries sensory information up.
options: That would be a tract named brain region first and "-spinal" second.
A tract named for a brain region ends in that region, so it leaves the cord.
Correct. Origin first, destination second: this is an ascending tract.
Tracts run inside the CNS; axons leaving through the ventral roots belong to motor neurons, not to a tract.

q: This sequence traces a motor command from the brain to a leg muscle. Find the wrong step.
options: The command leaves the motor areas of the cerebral cortex in a descending tract
It runs down the white columns of the spinal cord
It reaches motor neurons in the dorsal horn of a lumbar segment
Their axons leave through the ventral root toward the muscle

why.correct: Motor neurons to skeletal muscle sit in the ventral (anterior) horn, not the dorsal horn. The dorsal horn is the sensory side, where many incoming sensory axons end.
options: Right. Motor commands travel down in descending tracts.
Right. Tracts run in the white columns.
This is the error. The motor neurons are in the ventral horn.
Right. Motor axons leave through the ventral root.

q: Fill the gap in the sensory route into the cord: sensory neuron cell body in the dorsal root ganglion → dorsal root → ____ → neurons that relay the signal onward.
options: Dorsal horn
Ventral horn
Lateral horn
Ventral root

why.correct: Many sensory axons entering through the dorsal root end in the dorsal horn, on interneurons and on neurons that relay the signal up the cord.
options: Correct. Many incoming sensory axons end in the dorsal horn.
The ventral horn holds motor neurons, reached through interneurons, not directly by the dorsal root.
The lateral horn holds sympathetic motor neurons.
The ventral root carries motor axons out of the cord.

q: Which of these lies outside the central nervous system?
options: The ventral horn
The posterior column
The central canal of the spinal cord
The dorsal root ganglion

why.correct: The dorsal root ganglion sits on the dorsal root outside the spinal cord, so it is part of the peripheral nervous system. That is why its cluster of cell bodies is called a ganglion, not a nucleus.
options: The ventral horn is gray matter inside the spinal cord.
The posterior column is white matter inside the spinal cord.
The central canal runs through the middle of the spinal cord.
Correct. The dorsal root ganglion lies outside the cord.

q: Why does a newborn's spinal cord end at about the third lumbar vertebra, lower than an adult's?
options: The cord shrinks after birth as neurons die
The vertebral column keeps growing longer than the cord after birth
The conus medullaris moves up as the meninges tighten
Newborns have extra lumbar vertebrae that later fuse

why.correct: Early in fetal life the cord fills the whole canal. From then on the vertebral column grows faster and longer than the cord, so the cord's end sits relatively higher with age: about L3 at birth and L1–L2 in adults.
options: The cord does not shrink; it grows more slowly than the column.
Correct. Unequal growth leaves the cord ending higher in the canal.
The meninges do not pull the cord up; its end rises only because the column outgrows it.
Newborns have the same five lumbar vertebrae; it is the sacral vertebrae that fuse.
